item.title: I lost a state championship to a boy. I refuse to lose my voice
item.description: A Minnesota softball player describes losing her state championship semifinal to a team with a transgender pitcher and her fight for female athletes.
item.content:encoded:
I have never been much of a crier.

So when my softball team lost in the semifinals of the Minnesota state tournament, I surprised even myself. I sobbed to my parents and family. I was devastated, confused, and hurt. But underneath it all was a sense of helplessness.

I was a senior, and my biggest goal was to make the state tournament and play alongside my younger sister. We made it. We battled through the tournament as underdogs. And then our season ended because the opposing team was allowed to put a boy in as the pitcher on a girls' team. His team went on to win the girls' high school state championship.

WE WERE FORCED TO COMPETE AGAINST A MALE. THE SUPREME COURT HAD OUR BACKS

I wasn't crying because we had simply lost a softball game. I was crying because I couldn't understand how the adults who were supposed to protect girls like me had allowed this to happen.

I later learned that his parents had changed his legal documents to reflect the opposite sex when he was a young boy. What shocked me even more was the realization that the adults around us—administrators, policymakers and legislators—had allowed it and left girls like me tossed aside, hurt and abandoned.

WHAT'S NEXT IN THE BATTLE TO 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' AFTER SCOTUS RULING — AND THE HIDDEN DAMAGE DRIVING IT

We were expected to accept it, play through it and remain quiet.

But the consequences didn't stop with my team. When a male athlete advances through a girls' state tournament, every girl who might have faced that team is affected. Every roster spot, inning, championship, award and recruiting opportunity matters. At the elite level, one tournament can change a player's future. The impact extends across girls' teams throughout an entire state.

RILEY GAINES: SUPREME COURT HANDS WOMEN AN IMPORTANT WIN, BUT THE FIGHT ISN’T OVER

After our loss, I decided I wasn't going to stay quiet. I never imagined that decision, or that loss on a softball field in Minnesota, would eventually bring me to Washington, D.C. On Wednesday, I spoke at a press conference on Capitol Hill following a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on opportunity, fairness and safety for female athletes.

Getting to this point has not been easy. My decision to openly share my experience has come at a price.

DEMOCRAT SENATORS FLEE OR NO-SHOW JUDICIARY COMMITTEE HEARING ON PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS

I was recruited to play Division I softball at Western Michigan University. I entered college hoping to find my voice and pursue my dreams as a student-athlete. Instead, I felt isolated and shamed for speaking publicly about what I had experienced. I was even directed not to identify my university to the media. The message was clear: Keep quiet.

I believed then, and still believe now, that girls should not have to surrender roster spots, playing time or championships to boys because some adults have decided that the feelings of boys mean more than the feelings and opportunities of girls.

JONATHAN ALPERT: WOMEN WERE TOLD TO SPEAK UP. EXCEPT ABOUT WOMEN’S SPORTS

In an introductory sociology class, I was assigned a paper explaining the difference between sex and gender. I received a zero. My professor told me to "remove any bias and dive deeper into the difference between the two." She was telling me I was wrong to treat sex and gender as synonyms and that a person could identify as another gender by adopting stereotypes associated with the opposite sex. 

Confusing? Yeah, I know. I felt like I was being asked to erase my own perspective and accept something I believed was untrue as fact. I won't accept that women can be defined by sexist stereotypes. This wasn't just a classroom debate. I had lived it.

The lack of support from my coaches and the pressure in my coursework led me to transfer after my freshman season.

THESE FEMALE ATHLETES NEED TO SPEAK UP ABOUT KEEPING WOMEN'S SPORTS FOR WOMEN, LIKE SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM DID

Today, I play softball at Colorado Christian University. I feel supported, encouraged to speak out and, most importantly, unashamed to tell the truth about what happened to me.

I am now a sophomore in college, but I still think about that girl crying after the state tournament. I think about my younger sister, my cousins and all the girls coming after us.

I WAS A FEMALE ATHLETE, NOW I FIGHT FOR THEM IN COURT. WE NEED MORE SOPHIE CUNNINGHAMS

I can't change what happened on that field or give my team back the opportunity we lost. But I can refuse to let that loss teach the next generation of girls that they have to accept being pushed aside.

I want my sister and little cousins to grow up knowing that when adults fail to protect girls, girls can still find the courage to protect one another.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

I just wish we didn't have to.

I lost a state championship to a boy. I refuse to let girls lose their voice, too.

item.title: Minnesota coach PJ Fleck wipes player's blood all over his face after Gophers win over Washington
item.description: PJ Fleck smeared linebacker Maverick Baranowski's blood across his own cheeks after Minnesota's 27-24 road win at Washington on Saturday night.
item.content:encoded:
It's safe to assume that Minnesota head football coach PJ Fleck had an out-of-body experience after his Gophers earned a 27-24 win on the road at Washington on Saturday night.

Minnesota dominated much of the first half and took a 21-10 lead into the break before the Huskies managed to get back into the contest in the fourth quarter. Despite managing just two field goals in the second half, the Gophers held on and passed their first road test of the season.

After the final whistle, Fleck celebrated with his players on the field, but things went from routine celebration to absolutely insane when he crossed paths with linebacker Maverick Baranowski. The Gophers' leading tackler busted his lip during the game, and with blood still streaming down his chin, Fleck decided to wipe it with his hands and smear it across his cheeks.

Minnesota welcomes Michigan to town this upcoming Saturday in what will be a huge spot for both teams, with the Wolverines coming off of a stunning loss at home to Iowa in Week 4 and with the Gophers looking to make legitimate noise in the Big Ten.

item.title: One simple lifestyle choice could help you live longer, says longevity expert
item.description: Dan Buettner, founder of Blue Zones, says dog ownership may be the best longevity strategy, citing research linking it to fewer heart attacks and reduced loneliness.
item.content:encoded:
The most effective strategy for prolonging life might be at the end of a leash.

Dan Buettner, longevity expert and founder of the organization Blue Zones in Minneapolis, Minnesota, highlighted a growing body of scientific evidence showing that owning a dog is strongly associated with a reduced risk of early death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.

"The best thing you can do to add years to your life may surprise you. Get a dog!" Buettner advised during a recent episode of "The Dan Buettner Podcast." "Research shows that dog owners live longer, suffer fewer heart attacks and experience less loneliness. Why? Because a dog forces you to walk every day, gives you a purpose and provides unconditional love."

LEADING ONCOLOGIST REVEALS 6 HABITS THAT COULD PROMOTE LONGEVITY AND REDUCE YOUR RISK OF CHRONIC ILLNESS

Dog ownership is associated with a 24% reduction in all-cause mortality for the general population compared to non-owners, according to research published by the American Heart Association in its journal Circulation.

For individuals who have already suffered a major cardiac event, such as a heart attack or stroke, living with a dog reduced the risk of death by up to 33%.

Epidemiologists and psychologists point to three reasons why canine companions may extend human lifespans.

Studies published in BMC Public Health indicate that dog owners walk an average of 22 more minutes per day than non-owners, making them significantly more likely to meet standard weekly physical activity guidelines.

Interacting with a pet lowers levels of cortisol — the body’s primary stress hormone —while boosting oxytocin, dopamine and serotonin. A 12-year Swedish study analyzing 3.4 million participants found that dog owners had lower blood pressure and reduced rates of cardiovascular disease.

The U.S. Surgeon General has declared chronic loneliness a national public health epidemic, comparing its health risks to smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

Dogs act as natural "social catalysts," fostering community interaction and providing emotional attachment that combats isolation, particularly in single-person households, experts say.

The links between human longevity and caring for a pet aligns with principles found in the "blue zones" — regions of the world with the highest concentration of centenarians.

These key principles include natural daily movement, a strong sense of purpose, stress reduction and deep social connections, according to Buettner.

item.title: Trump's Greenland obsession isn’t random. Here’s what’s at stake
item.description: Greenland's untapped rare earth minerals, oil and gas reserves could reshape U.S. energy security as Trump's Denmark deal expands military presence.
item.content:encoded:
Greenland may be covered in ice, but beneath its surface could be resources critical to the global economy — including rare earth minerals, nickel, copper, palladium, cobalt, oil and natural gas.

The Arctic island’s location is just as valuable.

Positioned between North America and Europe, Greenland sits along key military and shipping routes. As conflicts in Ukraine and Iran expose vulnerabilities in global energy and supply chains, the island has become increasingly important to the United States and other world powers.

WHY TRUMP ZEROED IN ON GREENLAND, THE WORLD’S LARGEST ISLAND, MOSTLY COVERED IN ICE — IN 3 CHARTS

Those factors help explain why President Donald Trump has spent years pushing for greater American control and influence in Greenland and why his administration recently reached a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland.

The deal, which Trump signed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, will expand the U.S. military presence on the island while keeping Greenland under Danish sovereignty.

Here are three reasons Greenland has become one of the world’s most strategically important places.

The United States is seeking to reduce its dependence on China and Russia for critical minerals used in electronics, batteries, energy infrastructure and defense technology.

"We don’t want to be dependent on China for our rare earth minerals, and we don’t want to be dependent on Russia for them either," Robert Price, CEO of Greenland Energy Company and president of USFM Corporation, told Fox News Digital.

FLOURISH CHART EMBED HERE: 30309299

Price’s USFM is exploring nickel, copper, palladium and cobalt deposits around Disko Island in western Greenland. He said the region could eventually rival Russia’s mineral-rich Norilsk district, though its potential remains unproven as drilling continues.

Greenland’s potential riches extend beyond minerals. Price’s Greenland Energy Company is pursuing permits for an exploratory oil well planned for 2027 on the island’s eastern side, where he said the geology resembles the petroleum-producing North Sea.

"Our licenses are similar to the same petroleum system as the North Sea," Price said, adding that the company has sampled oil on and below the surface.

TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER

The project comes as the Iran war disrupts global energy markets and threatens shipping through the Strait of Hormuz a critical artery for the world’s oil supply.

"One of the reasons that we are exploring for oil in Greenland is because of what’s going on in the Strait of Hormuz right now," Price said.

Greenland’s oil and gas potential remains unproven and would require additional permits, exploration and investment.

Greenland’s strategic value also comes from its location between North America and Europe, near key air, sea and missile routes connecting the United States, Russia and Europe.

The U.S. has maintained a military presence on the island for decades. Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, is the northernmost Defense Department installation and supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance.

Melting Arctic ice is opening new shipping routes and increasing interest from the United States, Russia and China.

Trump’s agreement with Denmark and Greenland would expand the U.S. military presence while preserving Danish sovereignty, according to the administration. Price said the deal could also boost investor confidence in long-term oil, gas and mineral projects.

"What it does is it shores up long-term investment in Greenland, and that’s what our projects are," Price said. "They’re long-term investments from oil, gas and minerals."

item.title: Trump reaffirms ICE arrest policy after confusing guidance sparks alarm among agents
item.description: Trump told officials that anyone in the country illegally remains "on the table" for arrest and deportation after internal ICE guidance caused confusion.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration denied reports Saturday evening that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had temporarily instructed agents to limit arrests to illegal immigrants with criminal records.

The clarification comes as immigration enforcement remains a central pillar of President Donald Trump’s agenda. The administration has promised an aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration and expanded deportations, and officials said that effort has not been scaled back.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

Fox News correspondent Bill Melugin, who spoke with Trump and nine ICE and Department of Homeland Security sources, reported that verbal guidance instructing field offices to prioritize the "worst first" was distributed nationwide earlier this week.

The guidance alarmed some ICE agents, who described it as shocking and frustrating, Melugin wrote on X.

Sources later said the confusion stemmed from internal conversations about prioritizing the most serious offenders and that the directive was the result of a "miscommunication," rather than a formal change in policy.

"There is no change in immigration enforcement policy," Melugin wrote on X.

New guidance was sent to ICE field offices Saturday evening to reaffirm that the administration’s enforcement policy had not changed, according to the sources.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Trump told Fox News that ICE can still arrest and deport anyone who is in the country illegally.

ICE agents will also continue arresting illegal immigrants without additional criminal histories, including "collaterals," or individuals encountered during an operation targeting someone else.

The sources said the administration’s broader immigration enforcement agenda remains in place.
